title: 2 Samuel 11:1–5
context: In the spring, the season for military campaigns, David sends Joab and the army against Ammon but stays in Jerusalem himself. From his roof he sees a woman bathing, learns she is Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, sends messengers, and takes her. She later sends word that she is pregnant. The narrator tells the story briefly and soberly. Every verb of initiative belongs to David: he sends, inquires, takes and lies with her. The king holds the power, and the text never rebukes Bathsheba; in Nathan’s parable she will be pictured as the poor man’s lamb (12:3–4). Both traditions read this as David’s grave sin, an abuse of royal power by the man God had raised up, and neither tradition excuses him.

verses.text: At the return of the year, at the time when kings go out, David sent Joab and his servants with him, and all Israel; and they destroyed the children of Ammon and besieged Rabbah. But David stayed at Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
In spring, when kings go to war, David sends Joab and the army to fight Ammon and besiege Rabbah, but David stays in Jerusalem. The contrast is pointed.

Arminian readers note that the narrator quietly marks David’s absence from where a king was expected to be, and that idleness and neglected duty can open the door to temptation for anyone, however richly blessed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the man after God’s own heart (1 Samuel 13:14), richly blessed in chapters 5–10, is shown to be still a sinner in need of grace, and that no past faithfulness makes a believer immune to grave sin.

Both traditions read the verse as the quiet setting for a fall that David alone is responsible for.

verses.text: At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king’s house. From the roof, he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful to look at.
verses.arminianNotes:
One evening David rises from his bed, walks on the roof of the palace, and sees a very beautiful woman bathing. The narrator states only what David saw.

Arminian readers note that seeing was not yet sin, but David’s lingering look became the first step of a chosen path, and Scripture elsewhere warns that desire, when it conceives, gives birth to sin (James 1:14–15).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the narrator places the gaze with David, not with the woman, and that the heart’s desires, unchecked by grace, lead to outward acts, as Jesus taught about lust (Matthew 5:28).

Both traditions agree the verse does not fault Bathsheba, who was bathing as was ordinary, and that the responsibility lies with the king.

verses.text: David sent and inquired after the woman. One said, “Isn’t this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, Uriah the Hittite’s wife?”
verses.arminianNotes:
David sends to ask about the woman and is told she is Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam and wife of Uriah the Hittite. The answer should have stopped him.

Arminian readers note that David is given clear knowledge that she is another man’s wife, so his next act is a deliberate choice against God’s command (Exodus 20:14, 17), not a sin of ignorance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Eliam and Uriah both appear among David’s mighty men (23:34, 39), and if this is the same Eliam, the betrayal of loyal servants is even more grievous; the identification is likely but not certain.

Both traditions see the information as an unheeded warning that heightens David’s guilt.

verses.text: David sent messengers, and took her; and she came in to him, and he lay with her (for she was purified from her uncleanness); and she returned to her house.
verses.arminianNotes:
David sends messengers, takes her, lies with her, and she returns home; the narrator notes she had purified herself from her uncleanness. The verbs of action are David’s.

Arminian readers note that David uses royal power to take what is not his, and that the brief, sober telling refuses to dwell on the act while making the abuse of power plain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the purification remark is commonly read as referring to the end of her monthly period (compare Leviticus 15:19–28), which would show the child could only be David’s; it is not presented as a fault in her.

Both traditions place the guilt on David, the king who took another man’s wife, and do not blame Bathsheba.

verses.text: The woman conceived; and she sent and told David, and said, “I am with child.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The woman conceives and sends word to David that she is pregnant. Her only recorded words are a brief, urgent message.

Arminian readers note that Bathsheba’s message places the matter where responsibility lies, with David, and that sin hidden in private soon begins to bear consequences that cannot be concealed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the pregnancy confronts David with a choice between confession and concealment, and that his heart, left to itself, chooses concealment, showing how sin entangles further. Bathsheba is vulnerable, and the narrative gives her no rebuke.

Both traditions see this verse as the turning point at which David could have repented but did not.
